extracted.intended_audience: improv performers and students learning UCB long-form techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating the 'Game of the Scene' in UCB-style long-form improv: establishing a base reality, identifying a First Unusual Thing (FUT), framing and agreeing on it, developing a repeatable pattern, and heightening each beat logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes-And (establish Base Reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yes-And to establish a Base Reality
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and build on offers to create a grounded, normal world for the scene. Use 'Yes-And' to set the Base Reality early so unusual elements will stand out against a clear baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base Reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounded, normal world of the scene
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, consistent Base Reality gives context for the First Unusual Thing and makes the game's logic intelligible to performers and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Unusual Thing (FUT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice the first unusual element in the scene (First Unusual Thing, FUT)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the earliest deviation from Base Reality; the FUT is the seed of the scene's Game and should be recognized quickly so it can be framed and developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the unusual thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Call out and acknowledge the unusual thing — 'frame' it
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the FUT explicit through dialogue or behavior so partners and the audience understand what the scene's pattern will revolve around.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agree on the unusual thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Both partners accept and agree on the unusual element
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual agreement (acceptance and commitment) is necessary to make the FUT a shared premise that can be developed into a pattern; disagreement or ignoring the FUT kills the Game.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop into a patterned, repeatable Game
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the unusual element into a patterned, repeatable Game
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create recognizable beats or a repeatable behavior based on the FUT so the audience can anticipate and appreciate heightening and callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightening the Game
rubrics_metrics.description: Each iteration of the game should escalate
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logical extensions of the unusual premise to escalate — ask 'If this unusual thing is true, what else is true?' Avoid simply repeating the same beat; each beat should add stakes, specificity, or a larger consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: If-this-is-true reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Players should use 'if this is true, then what else is true...' reasoning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drive scenes by following logical (or comically logical) consequences of the FUT. This counterfactual/logical extension is the engine for discovery and heightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why the unusual thing makes sense (justification)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasons or context that make the FUT feel plausible within the scene's Base Reality; justification helps the audience buy into escalating absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern recognition and extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot and extend the pattern — recognize the Game and build on it
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Players should notice the emerging pattern and deliberately extend it in new, logical directions rather than ignoring or breaking the pattern arbitrarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore rather than repeat
rubrics_metrics.description: The unusual thing should be explored, not just repeated
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rote repetition of the same joke or beat; focus on exploration (new angles, escalations, consequences) so the Game continues to evolve and remain engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric checklist for evaluating a scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evaluative questions: 1) Is there a clear Base Reality? 2) Was the First Unusual Thing identified? 3) Is the game framed and agreed upon? 4) Does each beat heighten the game logically? 5) Are the players using 'if this is true, then what else...' reasoning? 6) Is the unusual thing being explored, not just repeated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these six questions as a concise evaluation tool to judge whether a scene successfully finds and develops its Game. Failures on any item indicate specific weaknesses (e.g., no FUT, lack of agreement, flat beats, or mere repetition).
